title: Objects in depth
summary: Unpack, spread and copy objects and arrays, and understand which names share one object.

misconceptions.description: Believes a destructuring default is ignored when the property is missing.
Believes array destructuring matches names to properties or values instead of positions.
Believes a function receives the elements of an array argument one by one without spread.
Believes a rest parameter holds a single argument instead of collecting all the remaining ones.
Believes spreading an array inside a call or literal still leaves it as one array.
Believes assigning an object to another variable, or spreading it, copies the nested data or shares nothing.
Believes a function receives a copy of an object argument.
Believes === on objects is true whenever their contents match.
Believes a spread copy also duplicates nested arrays and objects.
Reads the value a variable has at the end of the program for every earlier step.
Believes a destructuring default replaces the value even when the property exists.
Believes writing an object name inside braces adds its properties, as a spread would.
Believes assigning to a property through a second variable has no effect on the object.
Reads the value after an earlier call of the function than the one asked about.
Believes assigning a newly spread array to a property still leaves it sharing the original array.

conceptCard.title: Taking values out of arrays and objects
conceptCard.body: Destructuring reads several values in one line. An array pattern with square brackets matches by position. An object pattern with braces matches by property name. A default after = is used when the value is undefined, such as a missing property, and may use names set earlier. { key: name } stores it under another name.

conceptCard.title: Spread out, rest in
conceptCard.body: Three dots, two jobs. Spread expands an array in a call or array literal, and an object in an object literal. In a parameter list or a pattern, rest collects the remaining pieces into an array, or an object for an object pattern. A repeated key keeps its later value. In objects, { saved } means { saved: saved }.

conceptCard.title: Two names, one object
conceptCard.body: Objects and arrays are stored once, and a variable holds a reference to them. Assigning it to another name shares the object. Changing it through either name is seen by both. Methods such as push and reverse change an array in place. Strict equality asks whether two names reach the same object.

conceptCard.title: Copies one level deep
conceptCard.body: Spread makes a new object or array, but only for the top level. Plain values are copied. Nested objects and arrays are still shared between the copy and the original. A deep copy also copies those nested levels; to change a nested value safely, copy that level too.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. tip exists in bill, so its default is unused. note is missing, so it takes "none".
You thought a default always replaces the value. A default only steps in for a property that gives nothing to use.
You thought a default is ignored when the property is missing. A default exists for exactly the case where there is no value.

items.explanation: Destructuring matches properties by name. who and tip exist in bill, so they keep their values and the default 3 is unused. note is missing, so its default "none" is used.
hints: Look at lines 2 and 3: tip and note both have a default.
A default applies only when the value is undefined, for example a property the object lacks.
Check which of who, tip and note exist in bill.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Line 2 destructures an array. Which statement explains what the program prints?

options.text: Names are filled from the array in order, so silver gets the element at index 1.
options.feedback: Right. The second name in the pattern receives the second element, so the program prints Lee.

options.text: Each name is looked up as a property of the array, so silver is undefined.
options.feedback: You read the names as property names, as braces would. Square brackets in a pattern do not look names up on the array.

options.text: The names are matched against the element values, so silver is undefined.
options.feedback: You thought each name is compared with the element values. A name in the pattern is only a new variable; it does not search for anything.

items.explanation: An array pattern gives each name the element at the same position, starting from index 0. silver is the second name, so it receives board[1]. The names themselves play no role in the match.
hints: Compare the names on line 2 with the elements of board.
An array pattern has no property names to match. Think about what else can decide the match.
Count how many names come before silver in the pattern.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: What value does hi hold right after line 2 has run?

options.feedback: Right. lo is 2, and the missing hi takes its default lo + 1.
You used the default 6 for lo, as if a default always applied. A default only fills in a property the object does not have.
You thought hi's default is skipped because bag has no hi. A default is exactly what a missing property receives.

items.explanation: lo exists in bag, so it holds 2 and its default 6 is unused. hi is missing, so its default runs, and it reads the lo that is already set. 2 + 1 gives 3.
hints: Follow lo and then hi through line 2.
A default applies only when the property is missing. Names are filled from left to right.
Decide what lo holds before hi's default is worked out.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Complete line 2 so that the program prints the distance in kilometres.

options.feedback: Right. The property km holds 9 and is stored in distance.
That reads the path property, so the program prints Elm.
hike has no property called distance, so the variable is undefined.
hike is the object, not one of its properties, so the variable is undefined.

hints: Look at the property names on line 1.
In { name: variable } the left side is the property to read and the right side is the new variable.
Check the value stored under each property and pick the one that is a distance.

items.prompt: The program should print north and then south. Tap the buggy line, then choose its fix.

options.feedback: Right. Square brackets read the elements by position.
The names are in the wrong places. The name written first in the brackets gets the item at index 0, so the output order changes.
lanes[0] is the text "north". Destructuring a string reads its letters, so first is "n" and second is "o".

items.explanation: Line 2 uses an object pattern on an array. The array has no properties called first or second, so both are undefined. An array pattern with square brackets reads positions 0 and 1 and prints the lane names.
hints: Compare the brackets on line 2 with the value on its right.
Curly braces read properties by name; square brackets read positions.

items.prompt: Write the body of receiptLine(item). item has name, price and maybe qty (missing means 1). Return name, colon, space, then price times qty, as one text.
items.explanation: Destructuring item gives name, price and qty as variables, and the default 1 is used only when qty is missing. The line total is price * qty, and a template literal joins it to the name. A qty of 0 stays 0.
hints: Pull the properties out of item first.
An object pattern lists the property names between curly braces, and = gives a value for a missing property.
Only one of the three properties may be missing; decide how the pattern should treat it.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. Only the spread call passes the numbers one by one; the plain call passes one array.
You thought a plain array argument arrives as its elements. Without ..., a call receives the array as a single value.
You thought ... leaves the array in one piece. In a call, ... hands over the elements as separate arguments.

items.explanation: joined.push(...extra) spreads the array into two arguments, so joined gets two values. boxed.push(extra) passes one array, so boxed gets one value.
hints: Compare the two push calls on lines 3 and 5.
Spread turns an array into separate arguments; without it the array is one argument.
push adds one value for each argument it receives.

items.prompt: Which statement explains how tally treats its arguments?

options.text: scores collects every argument after label into one array.
options.feedback: Right. The rest parameter holds [4, 7], so its length is 2.

options.text: scores holds only the next argument after label.
options.feedback: You thought a rest parameter holds a single argument, the one next to label. A plain parameter already does that.

options.text: scores holds only the last argument that is passed.
options.feedback: You thought each extra argument replaces the one before it. Arguments are matched to parameters by position; none is overwritten.

items.explanation: A rest parameter written with ... gathers every argument that has no name of its own into one array. label takes "quiz", and scores becomes [4, 7], so its length is 2 and the function returns "quiz2".
hints: Look at the parameter list of tally on line 1.
A parameter written with three dots behaves differently from a normal parameter.
The call passes three arguments; the first goes to label. Where do the others go?

items.prompt: What value does route hold right after line 4 has run for the first time?

options.feedback: Right. After the first pass only the first leg has been added.
You thought spreading leg leaves it as one nested array. Inside [ ], ... places the elements of leg one by one, not leg itself.
That is the value after the last pass. The question asks about the first visit to line 4.

items.explanation: On the first pass leg is ["Ayr"]. Line 4 builds a new array from the elements of route and the elements of leg, so route becomes ["Bonn", "Ayr"]. The second leg is added only on the next pass.
hints: Follow route through the first pass of the loop only.
Spreading an array inside [ ] puts its elements, not the array, into the new array.
Check what route holds before the first pass and what leg is on that pass.

items.prompt: Order the lines so that the merged drink prints L, then 1.
items.explanation: The merged object needs both source objects, so it comes after them. The two declarations may swap. In the merge the later spread, order, overrides size with "L" while oat stays 1.

When two spreads share a key, the later one wins.

items.prompt: The saved volume 8 should win over the default. Tap the buggy line, then choose its fix.

options.feedback: Right. saved is spread last, so its volume replaces the default.
This adds one new property named saved that holds the whole object. opts.volume stays 5.
Spreading plain objects into an array literal is an error, because objects cannot be spread there.

items.explanation: Spread copies properties in order, so a key that appears in both objects takes its value from the later spread. Line 3 spreads saved first and base last, so the default 5 overwrites the saved 8.
hints: Look at the order of the two spreads on line 3.
When two spread objects share a key, the one written later wins.
Decide which of base and saved must come later for volume to end up as 8.

items.prompt: Write the body of withDefaults(saved). Return a new object that starts from volume 5 and muted false, with every property of saved on top of those.
items.explanation: Spread copies every property of saved into the new object. When a key appears twice, the later one wins, so saved must come after the defaults to override them. Spreading it first lets the defaults win.
hints: The new object holds the defaults and the properties of saved.
Spread puts every property of an object into a new one. When a key repeats, the later one wins.
Decide which of the two sources must come later in the literal.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. There is only one object, and both names lead to it.
You thought line 2 makes a second object for gift, so the change stays on gift. Assigning an object to another name builds no new object.
You expected both names to still read red. Line 3 assigns to a property of the object that mug and gift both lead to.

items.prompt: Which statement explains what the program prints?

options.text: === is true only for the very same object, not for equal contents.
options.feedback: Right. cardA and cardC share one object; cardB is a separate one.

options.text: === compares properties, so both comparisons are true.
options.feedback: You thought === looks inside objects and compares their properties. For objects it asks about the objects themselves, not their contents.

options.text: cardC is a copy of cardA, so both comparisons are false.
options.feedback: You thought line 3 builds a new object for cardC. Assigning an object only hands over what the variable holds; no new object appears.

items.explanation: === on two objects is true only when both names refer to the very same object. cardA and cardB were created separately, so the result is false even though their contents match. cardC is a second name for cardA, so that comparison is true.
hints: Look at lines 1 to 3: which names were given braces, and which was not?
=== treats objects differently from numbers and strings. Ask what it checks for objects.
Count how many pairs of braces create an object in lines 1 to 3.

items.prompt: What value does box hold right after line 8 has run?

options.feedback: Right. Each call changes the one shared object, so two calls add 2.
You thought bump gets a copy of box and changes only that. bump has two parameters, and a number and an object do not behave alike.
That is the value after line 7, the first call. The question asks about line 8, after the second call.

items.explanation: box is an object, so both calls to bump change the very same object: n goes 5, then 6, then 7. The number visits is copied into num, so changing num never affects visits. After line 8 box is {n: 7}.
hints: Look at lines 7 and 8: what can each call to bump change?
A function receives the same object, but a plain number is copied.
Count the calls that have run by line 8 and what line 5 does in each.

items.prompt: Which statement explains what the program prints?

options.text: Spread copies only the top level, so both objects share one sides array.
options.feedback: Right. The array was not duplicated, so the push is visible through both names.

options.text: Spread copies nested arrays too, so menu.sides still has length 1.

items.prompt: Write the body of addTag(shop, tag). shop has an id and a tags array. Return [copy, shop]: copy is shop with tag appended to its tags; shop is unchanged.
items.explanation: A spread copy shares its tags array with shop, so pushing onto it would also change shop. Building a new array with [...shop.tags, tag] and putting it in the copy leaves shop unchanged.
hints: Look at what happens to shop.tags if you push onto it.
A spread copy shares nested arrays with the original, so give the copy its own tags array.
The copy needs a tags array of its own that is not shop.tags.
